reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / standard metabolic references
clinicalPearls: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficient activity of the enzyme alpha-galactosidase A, leading to accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) in vascular endothelium and other tissues
Hemizygous males are typically most severely affected, but heterozygous females can develop significant disease because of variable X-inactivation
Childhood often begins with episodic burning pain in the hands and feet (acroparaesthesias) that may be provoked by fever, heat, or exercise
Angiokeratomas are clusters of small dark-red skin lesions, classically over the lower trunk and groin (bathing-trunk distribution)
A whorl-like corneal opacity (cornea verticillata) is a common and useful ophthalmological clue that usually does not impair vision
Reduced or absent sweating (hypohidrosis) contributes to heat intolerance and unexplained fevers
Progressive involvement of the kidneys, heart, and cerebrovascular system in adulthood causes renal failure, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, and early stroke
Enzyme replacement therapy and, for eligible variants, an oral pharmacological chaperone can stabilise disease, and adjunctive treatments target pain and organ protection
reference.pathophysiology: Fabry disease is caused by pathogenic variants in the GLA gene on the X chromosome, which encodes lysosomal alpha-galactosidase A. Deficient enzyme activity prevents cleavage of terminal galactose from globotriaosylceramide (Gb3), causing progressive glycosphingolipid accumulation within lysosomes, most notably in vascular endothelial and smooth muscle cells, renal podocytes and tubular cells, cardiomyocytes, and neurons. This storage triggers endothelial dysfunction, a prothrombotic and pro-inflammatory state, and progressive fibrosis of the kidney, heart, and brain vasculature, producing the multisystem adult phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of neuropathic limb pain such as small-fibre neuropathy
Rheumatological or 'growing pains' misattribution in childhood
Other lysosomal storage disorders with multisystem involvement
Hereditary hypertrophic cardiomyopathy from other causes
Other inherited causes of chronic kidney disease and proteinuria
additionalInvestigations: Plasma or leukocyte alpha-galactosidase A activity, most reliable in males
GLA molecular genetic testing, essential for diagnosis in females
Plasma or urinary Gb3 and lyso-Gb3 biomarkers
Urinalysis and renal function including proteinuria assessment
Cardiac evaluation with ECG and echocardiography, and slit-lamp examination for cornea verticillata
redFlags: Unexplained early stroke or transient ischaemic attack in a young patient
Progressive proteinuria or declining renal function
Left ventricular hypertrophy, arrhythmia, or heart failure
Severe pain crises interfering with function and quality of life
reference.prognosis: Untreated classic disease progresses to end-stage renal disease, cardiac complications, and premature stroke, shortening life expectancy. Early initiation of enzyme replacement or chaperone therapy, together with organ-directed supportive care, can slow progression and improve outcomes, though established fibrosis is not reversible.
pitfalls: Dismissing childhood limb pain as growing pains and delaying diagnosis for years
Relying on enzyme activity alone to exclude the disease in females, in whom levels can be normal
Overlooking cornea verticillata that could prompt earlier recognition
Failing to screen and counsel at-risk relatives given X-linked inheritance
